title: Intro to Higher Math
pitch: This course is designed to bridge the gap between school mathematics, which primarily focuses on computation and problem-solving techniques, and the demands of university-level mathematics.
overview: Mathematics is the language of science, engineering, and computing. While school mathematics focuses on computation and techniques, university mathematics emphasizes abstraction, logical reasoning, and mathematical proof.

This course bridges that transition by introducing the language and foundations of higher mathematics, including sets, functions, proof techniques, combinatorics, and elementary number theory. Students will develop the mathematical thinking and problem-solving skills needed for further study.
By the end of the course, students will be prepared for subsequent courses in calculus, linear algebra, discrete mathematics, graph theory, probability, and other mathematically intensive subjects.
highlights: Master essential concepts such as sets, functions, and their properties
Develop proficiency in key proof techniques
Build skills in combinatorics, elementary number theory, vectors, polynomials, and complex numbers
Strengthen logical reasoning, abstraction, and clear mathematical communication
prerequisites: There are no special prerequisites for this course. A solid background in high school mathematics is recommended.
methodology: Lectures, guided problem-solving, interactive discussions, individual practice, and collaborative group activities. Each session introduces new concepts through worked examples, followed by exercises designed to develop mathematical reasoning and problem-solving skills.
Active participation is essential. Students regularly discuss solution strategies, present and explain their reasoning, and work in groups to compare approaches.

Proof is the central theme: students explain the reasoning behind solutions rather than present final answers. AI tools are permitted as a learning aid, but all submitted work must reflect the student's own understanding and every solution must be explainable on demand.

sessionShape.note: 3 contact hours. Default rhythm used by the deck generator.

blocks.name: Warm-up
blocks.purpose: Recall + one question that the day's idea answers

blocks.name: Concept I
blocks.purpose: Definitions, worked examples on the board

sessions.title: Course overview and School math refresher
sessions.goal: Set expectations for a proof-based course and re-arm the algebraic toolkit everything else stands on.
objectives: State how this course differs from school maths: claims need justification, not just answers
Fluently manipulate exponents, radicals, fractions, absolute value and inequalities
Factor and complete the square; solve quadratic equations and inequalities
Read and write basic mathematical notation and quantifier-free statements precisely
boardExamples: Why (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 is a theorem, not a rule to memorise
Solve |2x - 3| < 5 and justify each step as an equivalence
Complete the square on x^2 - 6x + 13 and read off the minimum
pitfalls: Treating sqrt(x^2) as x rather than |x|
Multiplying an inequality by a quantity of unknown sign
Writing chains of '=' between things that are not equal
sessions.homework: Diagnostic set: 12 algebra/inequality items, each answer accompanied by one sentence of justification.

sessions.title: Sets & set operations
sessions.goal: Introduce sets as the common language of all later topics, and set identities as the first real proofs.
objectives: Use roster and set-builder notation; distinguish element-of from subset
Compute union, intersection, difference, complement, symmetric difference and Cartesian product
Prove set equalities by double inclusion and by element-chasing
Compute power sets and state |P(A)| = 2^|A|
boardExamples: Prove A \ (B ∩ C) = (A \ B) ∪ (A \ C) by double inclusion
List P({1,2,3}) and count it
Show A × B ≠ B × A in general, with the smallest counterexample
pitfalls: Assuming a Venn diagram is a proof
Forgetting that the empty set is a subset of every set
sessions.homework: Set identities: 6 to prove by double inclusion, 3 to disprove by counterexample.

sessions.title: Functions
sessions.subtitle: Trigonometric functions.
sessions.goal: Move from 'formula' to 'function': domain, codomain, rule - and the injective/surjective/bijective vocabulary.
objectives: Define a function as a rule with a specified domain and codomain; distinguish codomain from image
Decide and prove injectivity, surjectivity, bijectivity
Compose functions and construct inverses of bijections
Define sine, cosine, tangent on the unit circle; read off period, domain, range and the basic identities
boardExamples: f(x) = x^2 is not injective on R but is on [0, ∞): show both
Prove that if g∘f is injective then f is injective
Derive sin^2 θ + cos^2 θ = 1 from the unit circle
pitfalls: Saying 'the function x^2' without stating a domain
Confusing the inverse function with the reciprocal
Working in degrees when the definition assumed radians
sessions.homework: Injective/surjective classification (8 items with proof or counterexample) + 5 unit-circle values derived, not recalled.

sessions.title: Function families (polynomial, exp/log, trig)
sessions.goal: Build a mental library of standard functions and their growth, so later arguments can reason by shape.
objectives: Classify polynomial functions by degree; describe end behaviour and root count
State and use the laws of exponents and logarithms; convert between bases
Compare growth rates: logarithmic < polynomial < exponential
Transform graphs by shift, scale and reflection, and recognise trig functions as periodic models
boardExamples: Show log_b(x) = ln x / ln b and use it to compare log_2 n with log_10 n
Rank n, n log n, n^2, 2^n by eventual size and justify the ranking
Model daily temperature with A sin(ω t + φ) + C and identify each parameter
pitfalls: Writing log(a + b) = log a + log b
Reading 'exponential' as merely 'fast'
Applying a horizontal shift in the wrong direction
sessions.homework: Growth-comparison set, log manipulation, and one modelling question with written justification.

sessions.title: Theorem proving (direct, contrapositive, contradiction - disproof by counterexample)
sessions.goal: The pivot of the course: teach the standard proof templates and when each one is the right tool.
objectives: Parse implications, converses, contrapositives; use ∀ and ∃ correctly
Write a direct proof with an explicit hypothesis and conclusion
Choose contraposition when the negation is the easier hypothesis
Run a proof by contradiction, and disprove a universal claim with one counterexample
boardExamples: Direct: the sum of two even integers is even
Contrapositive: if n^2 is even then n is even
Contradiction: sqrt(2) is irrational
Counterexample: 'every prime is odd' fails at 2
pitfalls: Proving the converse by accident
Assuming the conclusion inside the proof
Negating a quantified statement incorrectly (¬∀x P is ∃x ¬P)
Offering examples as proof of a universal statement
sessions.homework: 8 claims: prove or disprove, each with the technique named at the top of the solution.

sessions.title: Mathematical induction
sessions.goal: Give students a proof method for infinitely many statements, and make them write the induction step honestly.
objectives: State the principle of induction and identify base case, hypothesis, inductive step
Prove summation identities and divisibility claims by induction
Use strong induction where the n-1 case is not enough
Recognise failed inductions (missing base case, hypothesis never used)
boardExamples: Prove 3 divides n^3 - n for all n ≥ 1
Strong induction: every integer n ≥ 2 has a prime factorisation
The 'all horses are the same colour' fallacy - locate the broken step
pitfalls: Verifying the base case for the wrong starting index
Writing the inductive step without ever invoking the hypothesis
Confusing 'assume true for n' with 'assume true for all n'
sessions.homework: 6 induction proofs, one of which must use strong induction, plus a broken proof to diagnose.

sessions.title: Elementary combinatorics and binomial theorem
sessions.goal: Teach counting as a modelling activity: name the objects, name the rule, then count.
objectives: Apply the sum and product rules; count with and without repetition
Distinguish permutations from combinations and compute both
State the binomial theorem and expand (a+b)^n; read Pascal's triangle
Prove simple identities combinatorially (double counting) as well as algebraically
boardExamples: How many 5-card hands contain exactly two aces?
Prove C(n,k) = C(n, n-k) both algebraically and by a bijection
Expand (x + 2)^5 with binomial coefficients
Pigeonhole: among 13 people two share a birth month
pitfalls: Counting ordered arrangements when order does not matter (and vice versa)
Double counting overlapping cases without inclusion-exclusion
Treating identical objects as distinguishable
sessions.homework: 10 counting problems; each answer must state the counting rule used and why the cases are disjoint.

sessions.title: Midterm
sessions.goal: Assess sessions 1-7: sets, functions, function families, proof techniques, induction, counting.
objectives: Write correct, readable proofs under time pressure
Choose an appropriate proof technique unprompted
Compute accurately with sets, functions and counting rules
pitfalls: Answer-only solutions score poorly - the reasoning is the assessed object
sessions.homework: Post-midterm: each student writes a corrected version of one lost-mark problem.

sessions.title: GCD & divisibility
sessions.goal: Start number theory from the division algorithm and get to Bezout via the Euclidean algorithm.
objectives: State and use the definition a | b and the division algorithm
Run the Euclidean algorithm and the extended version
Prove basic divisibility lemmas directly from the definition
State the fundamental theorem of arithmetic and use gcd/lcm via factorisation
boardExamples: gcd(1071, 462) by the Euclidean algorithm, then Bezout coefficients
Prove: if a | b and a | c then a | (bx + cy) for all integers x, y
Show gcd(a,b) · lcm(a,b) = ab
pitfalls: Reading a | b backwards
Assuming remainders may be negative
Confusing 'coprime in pairs' with 'coprime as a set'
sessions.homework: Euclidean algorithm drills + 4 divisibility proofs from the definition.

sessions.title: Modular arithmetic
sessions.goal: Introduce congruence as an equivalence relation and arithmetic in Z_n, with real applications.
objectives: Define a ≡ b (mod n) and verify it is an equivalence relation
Add, subtract and multiply congruences; know when cancellation is legal
Find modular inverses via the extended Euclidean algorithm; solve linear congruences
Apply modular arithmetic: parity/divisibility tests, clock arithmetic, check digits, hashing
boardExamples: Compute 7^100 mod 13 by repeated squaring
Solve 14x ≡ 6 (mod 20) - and explain why solutions come in a family
Prove the divisibility-by-9 rule using 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9)
pitfalls: Dividing both sides of a congruence by a non-invertible element
Assuming every element of Z_n has an inverse
Sign errors on negative residues
sessions.homework: Congruence computation set + prove one divisibility rule + one small applied problem.

sessions.title: Vectors (2D, magnitude, dot product, ℝⁿ)
sessions.goal: Introduce vectors both geometrically and algebraically, and generalise the picture to n dimensions.
objectives: Add, subtract and scale vectors; compute magnitude and unit vectors
Compute the dot product and use it for angle and orthogonality
Project one vector onto another
Generalise the definitions to ℝⁿ and state Cauchy-Schwarz and the triangle inequality
boardExamples: Angle between (3,4) and (-4,3): why is it 90 degrees?
Project (5,2) onto (1,1) and decompose into parallel + perpendicular parts
Prove the triangle inequality from Cauchy-Schwarz
pitfalls: Treating the dot product as producing a vector
Forgetting to normalise before projecting
Assuming geometric intuition transfers to ℝⁿ without proof
sessions.homework: Dot-product computations, one projection problem, one proof using Cauchy-Schwarz.

sessions.title: Polynomials
sessions.goal: Treat polynomials as algebraic objects: division, roots, factor theorem - the bridge to complex numbers.
objectives: Perform polynomial long division and synthetic division
Use the remainder and factor theorems to find and verify roots
Apply the rational root theorem and Vieta's formulas
Relate multiplicity of roots to the factorisation and to the graph
boardExamples: Divide x^4 - 3x^2 + 2 by x - 1 and read off the remainder two ways
Factor x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 using the rational root theorem
From Vieta: find the sum and product of the roots of 2x^2 - 5x + 3 without solving
pitfalls: Dropping the zero coefficient of a missing term during long division
Assuming every real polynomial factors over the reals
Confusing multiplicity with the number of distinct roots
sessions.homework: Division + factorisation set, plus one Vieta problem and one proof about degrees.

sessions.title: Complex numbers (roots, FTA, Euler / De Moivre)
sessions.subtitle: Estimate and example.
sessions.goal: Complete the number system: why C exists, how it computes, and what the fundamental theorem of algebra buys us.
objectives: Do arithmetic in C; use conjugate and modulus
Convert between rectangular and polar/exponential form
Apply De Moivre's theorem and find all n-th roots of a complex number
State the fundamental theorem of algebra and connect it to session 12's factorisation
boardExamples: Compute (1 + i)^8 in polar form in one line
Find all cube roots of 8 and plot them on the unit circle
Derive cos 3θ from De Moivre
e^{iπ} + 1 = 0 as a consequence, not a slogan
pitfalls: Losing roots by taking only the principal argument
Writing sqrt(-1)·sqrt(-1) = sqrt(1)
Forgetting that arg is defined modulo 2π
sessions.homework: Polar-form conversions, all n-th roots of two numbers, one De Moivre identity derived.

sessions.title: Course recap, why math is important in the era of AI, and preparing for the exam
sessions.goal: Tie the 13 topics into one narrative, argue why proof literacy matters more when machines produce answers, and rehearse the exam.
objectives: Trace the through-line: sets → functions → proof → induction → counting → number theory → vectors → polynomials → C
Articulate why verification, not generation, is the scarce skill in the AI era
Self-assess against the exam blueprint and target remaining gaps
Practise writing a full solution under exam conditions
boardExamples: A plausible-looking but wrong AI proof - students locate the broken step
Mixed-topic timed problem set with live marking rubric
pitfalls: Revising by re-reading rather than by re-proving
sessions.homework: Full mock exam under time, self-marked against the published rubric.

sessions.title: Final exam
sessions.goal: Assess the full course with an emphasis on proof and justification.
objectives: Produce correct and communicable proofs across the syllabus
Select techniques without prompting
Compute reliably in number theory, vectors, polynomials and complex numbers
